summary: Red Frontier is a Mars EVA planning and rehearsal console using NASA orbital and rover observations. Its example mission walks 723 m from a habitat to Mount Sharp's boxwork ridges, minerals left by ancient groundwater, to photograph and sample them, and the plan is approved only if return and rescue stay within limits. On a processed 2 m HiRISE terrain grid of Mount Sharp (Gale crater), it finds routes using a proposed safety-weighted cost and shows go/no-go checks for modeled return, partner rescue, time budgets, terrain, daylight and archived space weather. Slope margins come from a comparison with 508 Curiosity stops. Crews can propose habitats, refuges and depots, plan multi-stop sorties and multi-sol rover logistics across 48 candidate regions, and rehearse failures in a HUD. Radio coverage and terrain shadows are inspection tools. GPS-free localization compares Navcam skylines with terrain and can fuse manually entered pressure, travel, bearing and range measurements. A downloaded local copy, zone data and camera metadata support offline calculations. Human equipment, stock and failure rates remain modeled assumptions requiring calibration.
details:
What It Does

  • Martian map with real layers. 48 candidate human landing zones (NASA Exploration Zones in JPL Mars Trek), each with a 200 km region (MOLA–HRSC relief, THEMIS day IR) for rover planning, and a 5 × 10 km walking zone in Gale at 2 m from a HiRISE DTM: orthoimage, slope, roughness, THEMIS night IR (thermal), CRISM HYD/PHY (hydrated minerals and clays), Curiosity's traverse and photos.
  • Example science mission. One button loads a habitat and a science stop on Mount Sharp's boxwork ridges (minerals left by ancient groundwater), both placed at real Curiosity stops: a 723 m walk, 60 min of photos and sampling, and return. The itinerary is computed and approved (EVA GO) only if emergency return and partner rescue stay within limits.
  • Walking terrain and measured slope margin. Cells are classified against model limits. Comparing the map with rover tilt at 508 Curiosity stops gave a 5.84° 95th-percentile slope underestimation and a roughly 54 m registration offset. Subtracting that percentile from a 20° Artemis reference gives the code's rounded 14.2° limit. This is an own measurement against rover tilt, with lunar capability transferred to a Martian planning model.
  • Modeled return and rescue zone. From the departure base and eligible additional refuges, the engine computes two time fields (Dijkstra on the terrain): emergency return on secondary oxygen (≤ 60 min incl. 10 min ingress) and rescue of an incapacitated partner dragged at half speed on slopes ≤ 10° (≤ 60 min). Only cells that satisfy both enter the mask. Deadlines reference lunar operations. Half-speed dragging and the 10° rescue slope ceiling are team proposals to calibrate. Eligible refuges can expand the area, depending on terrain and overlap.
  • Weighted route search, manual tracing and itineraries. A* with a Tobler-type walking speed and penalties for slope, roughness, closeness to forbidden terrain and probable soft soil. The astronaut can also trace a route by hand (checked segment by segment) or chain several science stops; each plan gets a go / no-go card: every control shows its value, threshold and source (NASA reference, own measurement, or proposal to calibrate).
  • Routes through bases over several days and long rover expeditions. The planner chains habitats, refuges and depots with stock: each leg is approved on its own, legs are grouped into days with daylight, overnight stays and recharges deduct stock, and the card says "approved in N days via..."; if no chain works it says which leg fails and where a refuge would fix it. For distant targets it splits a pressurized-rover drive into sols, places overnight stops and tells how many energy depots and refuges must be pre-positioned.
  • EVA Window and HUD. Mars time (Mars24), the latest Curiosity REMS report and NASA DONKI space weather (CME arrivals at Mars, SEP events) drive a green/amber/red window. The HUD simulation walks the approved route, consumes modeled resources (primary/secondary O₂, CO₂ capacity, battery, cooling water) and shows a live point of no return. Injecting a leak, incapacitated partner, solar storm or lost comms requests a return path and checks its deadline.
  • GPS-free geolocation. Navcam skylines are extracted, converted to angles using CAHVOR camera metadata and rover attitude, and matched to HiRISE + MOLA–HRSC horizons. The stored blind test on 12 Curiosity stops has median error 20.1 m, with 9 inside their reported intervals. Extra readings (barometer, steps/bearing, odometry, radio/UWB range, landmark resection, Sun angles) are fused as independent likelihoods; the 95% region is a model credibility that needs empirical calibration.
  • Comparative probabilities. Automatic, manual and itinerary cards show first-failure probabilities using proposed rates, with the weakest stretches, to compare plans under the same assumptions.
  • Field tools. Right-click menu: measure distance, bearing and elevation profile, radio line-of-sight coverage, Sun position and shadows at selectable hours, coordinates and GeoJSON import/export. Solar timing was compared with 700 Curiosity sols (1,400 sunrise/sunset events), mean absolute error about 0.6 min. The app and its built-in guide are available in English and Spanish.

How It Works

  • Python pipeline (rasterio, NumPy, SciPy): downloads NASA/USGS products, reprojects them to a common Mars equirectangular grid (IAU 2000 sphere, planetocentric latitude, east longitude), derives slope and roughness, validates against Curiosity, extracts the Navcam skylines and caches space-weather and REMS data.
  • Web app in plain JavaScript modules and local Leaflet with no build step. Routing and optical localization run in Web Workers. Parameters live in configuration files with value, source and status (verified, own measurement, or proposal to calibrate).
  • Tests with the Node test runner cover routing, risk, localization, solar geometry, radio, barometry, consumables, reliability, simulation, planning and the bilingual guide; pytest covers the data pipeline.

Why It Matters

Planetary maps show what the ground looks like; astronauts need to know what they are allowed to do on it and how they get back. Red Frontier makes the safety reasoning explicit and auditable: it never hides a "no", it says which rule failed, and it separates real NASA data, modeled layers and team proposals. It is a planning aid, not a guarantee of safety.

Tools

Python 3.12 (rasterio/GDAL, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow), JavaScript (ES modules, Web Workers), Leaflet 1.9.4, Node.js test runner, pytest. Source code and data: https://github.com/Redi12312/red-frontier

AI Assistance

AI tools were used to translate the web interface into English, as a guide to find and summarize NASA research sources, and as a programming assistant for parts of the code, tests and explanatory texts. The team chose the scope, reviewed the results and tested them. All observations come from the cited NASA and USGS data sources; calculated layers, planning models and simulated equipment are labeled separately. No images, audio or video were generated with AI, and no NASA logos were used.
